transcript.content: Hi, welcome in—I'm Dr. [Name]. To start, can you tell me what brings you in today?

Hi, Doc. Well, I guess I'm here because... well, work's been hounding me to get checked out. I manage the whole operations floor over at the distribution center. Been there thirty years, started on the forklift back when I was just a teenager, barely out of middle school, and now I run the whole crew. It's a lot of moving parts, you know? Just last week we had this massive shipment of pallets come in late, totally screwed up the loading dock schedule for three days straight, and I had guys calling out left and right... 

But, uh, anyway, I was talking to my supervisor about the schedule and... I don't know, it just slipped out. I keep having these thoughts lately that my family might just be better off if I didn't wake up in the morning. And that actually scared me enough to tell him, which is saying something. So he told me I needed to come see you.
How long have you been feeling this way—when did you first start noticing this low mood or these thoughts, and has it been more or less constant since then?

Well, I guess... this whole change in me, it’s been going on for about two weeks now. Ever since my daughter left Georgia for the military. Which, you know, I’m incredibly proud of her. It’s a brave thing to do. 

My uncle was in the service, actually—Army Corps of Engineers. He used to tell me these crazy stories when I was a kid, back before I quit school to start at the warehouse. He was over in Korea, building bridges in the freezing cold, mud up to his knees. He actually lost two toes to frostbite. Used to take his boot off at Thanksgiving just to show us kids, which drove my mother absolutely up the wall. She’d be right in the middle of setting down the turkey, and there's Uncle Earl waving his foot around the dining room table... God, the yelling matches they'd get into over that. 

But, uh... what was I saying? Oh, right, the thoughts. Yeah, it's been about two weeks since she left. I'm sorry, did you ask something else just now? I kind of lost my train of thought.
Over these past two weeks, would you say you've been feeling down or losing interest in things you normally enjoy nearly every day, for most of the day?

Well, yeah, pretty much all day, every day. It's like... I just don't care about the stuff I usually do. Like, I used to love messing around with my tomato plants out back. I had these Cherokee Purples that were getting huge, and I'd spend hours out there. And sanding wood at my workbench, too. I was making this little birdhouse for my neighbor. He's got these blue jays that come around, meanest birds you ever saw. One of 'em swooped down and pecked his bald spot last summer while he was trying to mow the lawn. He had to run inside and put a band-aid on his head. Looked ridiculous. But he's a good guy, you know? Always brings my trash cans up from the curb if I'm working late at the warehouse. 

Anyway, I used to do all that, and watch the Falcons games, and stay after church just talking with folks... but lately, I don't know. I just look at the garden and the workbench and it's like... like it all belongs to somebody else. I just sit there. I don't even turn the TV on for the game anymore.
When you have these thoughts about your family being better off without you, have you thought about any specific way you might act on that, or do you have any intention to do so?

Well, no, I haven't... I haven't got a plan or anything like that. No intention to actually do it. It's just... like I told my supervisor, and that's why I'm here, I just keep having these thoughts that they'd all be better off if I just didn't wake up. It really scared me to even think it. 

I mean, my wife, she's got enough on her plate right now anyway. She's been trying to get the neighborhood association to fix the potholes on our street for, gosh, must be three years now. You wouldn't believe the runaround they give her. Last month, she finally got the city councilman on the phone—Jimmy Henderson, I went to school with his older brother, actually. The brother, Tommy, he used to drive this beat-up old Chevy Nova, loud as a freight train, and he'd do donuts in the Piggly Wiggly parking lot on Friday nights until the cops showed up. Tommy ended up moving out to Texas to work on the oil rigs, made a fortune, but Jimmy stayed here and got into politics. Always wore a suit, even in high school, which we all thought was a little weird. 

But anyway, she got Jimmy on the phone, and he promised he'd send a crew out, but of course, nobody ever showed. Typical, right? Just empty promises. So she's stressed about that, and the water heater's been making this awful clanking noise... 

Wait, I'm sorry, I'm doing it again, aren't I? What did you ask me? Oh, right, the thoughts. Yeah, no plan to do anything. Just... just the thoughts that they'd be better off without me.
Over these past two weeks, have you noticed any changes in your sleep—trouble falling asleep, staying asleep, or waking up much earlier than usual?

Well, I don't think my sleep has changed much, really. I mean, I still go to bed around the same time. Usually right after the ten o'clock news. Though lately, the news has just been so depressing, you know? All they talk about is the economy and those new subdivisions they're building out past the highway. 

They're tearing down all those old pecan orchards to put up these giant houses that all look exactly the same. My buddy Rick, he used to work for the developer doing the grading, and he said they don't even leave any of the good topsoil. Just scrape it all away. Rick actually found an old arrowhead out there once, right in the middle of where they were digging a foundation. Said it looked like it was made of quartz or something. He brought it into the warehouse to show me, had it sitting on his desk right next to his stapler for a whole year until his grandson accidentally knocked it into the trash can. Boy, was he mad about that. Didn't speak to the kid for a week. 

But, uh, sleep... no, I haven't really noticed any trouble with it. I just go to bed and wake up like normal, I guess.
Have you noticed any changes in your appetite or your weight over the past two weeks?

Well, yeah, actually. Most days I have to make myself eat even just a few bites. It's like I have zero interest in food right now. Even the stuff I normally like, you know? Like, at the warehouse, the guys always order from this barbecue place down on 4th Street on Fridays. Smitty's, it's called. Best pulled pork in the county, I swear. Smitty himself used to run the pit out back, big guy, always had a cigar in his mouth, even when he was flipping the ribs. 

He had this old bloodhound named Buster that used to sleep right next to the smoker. Laziest dog you ever saw. One time, a health inspector came by and tried to tell Smitty he couldn't have the dog back there. Smitty just looked at him, didn't say a word, just pointed at the door with his tongs until the guy left. We all laughed about that for weeks. Buster lived to be, gosh, must've been fifteen years old before he finally passed. Smitty actually closed the restaurant for a whole day when it happened. Put a little sign on the door and everything. 

But anyway, they ordered from there last Friday, and I just couldn't do it. The sandwich just sat on my desk all afternoon until I finally threw it in the trash. Same thing at home, really. My wife made her meatloaf on Tuesday, and I just pushed it around my plate. So yeah, I guess my appetite is pretty much gone.
Over these past two weeks, have you been feeling unusually worthless, or blaming yourself for things that aren't really your fault?

Well, yeah, I guess I have been feeling pretty down on myself. Especially about my daughter. She moved out a while back, and I just keep going over it in my head, telling myself I must have failed her somehow. Like, if I was a better father, I would have done something different, you know? 

She moved out to Seattle, actually. Said she wanted to be closer to the mountains or something. I don't know much about Seattle, except it rains all the time and they've got that big tower with the restaurant on top. My cousin Lou went up there for a convention once—he sells industrial floor buffers, mostly to hospitals and big schools. Lou said the coffee out there is so strong it'll put hair on your chest. He actually brought me back a bag of beans from some little roaster downtown, but I never got around to grinding them. I don't even own a coffee grinder. I just use the Folgers crystals, always have. My dad used to drink Folgers, too. He had this old tin mug he took with him every morning to the auto shop. He dropped a transmission on his foot once, right after he finished his coffee. Didn't even go to the hospital, just taped it up and kept working. Tough old bird, my dad. 

But, uh, yeah, my daughter... I just can't shake this feeling that it's my fault she left. Like I messed up somewhere along the line.
Over these past two weeks, have you noticed feeling unusually tired or low on energy, or having trouble concentrating on tasks at work?

Well, yeah, it's been real tough to focus. Like, at the distribution center, I'll be staring right at the schedule or the routing sheet, and my mind just won't lock in. It's like I'm looking at words but they don't mean anything. So even these little staffing calls, you know, figuring out who's on which shift, they just feel so much bigger and harder than they ought to. 

We had this one guy, Tommy, who used to do the scheduling before me. He was a real character. Always wore these bright yellow suspenders, said they helped him think better. He actually bought them at this little hardware store down in Florida when he was on vacation with his wife. They went to Panama City Beach every single year for their anniversary. Rented the exact same condo on the third floor. Tommy said the elevator in that building was so slow you could read a whole newspaper before you got to the lobby. He used to read the sports section on the way down, always checking the greyhound racing results. Not that he ever bet on them, he just liked the dogs' names. Some of them are real funny, you know? Like "Lightning Bug" or "Salty Biscuit." 

But yeah, I just can't seem to concentrate on the schedules lately. Just feels like my brain is moving through molasses or something.
Have these feelings and difficulties been severe enough that you've had trouble actually completing your work duties or handling your usual responsibilities at home?

Yeah, it's... it's gotten pretty bad, to be honest. At work, my mistakes started getting serious enough that my supervisor actually found me just sitting out in my truck before dawn one morning. He ended up getting occupational health involved, which was a whole embarrassing ordeal. I was just sitting in the cab, not even with the radio on, you know? 

It's a Chevy Silverado. Good truck. I bought it off this fella named Al over at the dealership on Route 9. Al was a real trip, he always wore these ridiculous neckties. The day I bought the truck, he had on this tie with little singing bass fish all over it. Reminded me of my brother-in-law, Gary. Gary is obsessed with fishing. He goes up to the lake every August, rents this little cabin that doesn't even have indoor plumbing. Just an outhouse out back. I told him he's crazy for paying good money to use a hole in the ground, but he says it builds character. He actually caught this massive catfish last year and had it stuffed and mounted right above his TV in the living room. His wife hates it, says its glass eyes follow her around when she's vacuuming. She tried to throw it out once when he was at work, but it wouldn't fit in the trash can. 

But, uh... anyway, what was I saying? Oh, right, my responsibilities. Yeah, it's the same thing at home, really. I’ve just let all the bills and my regular chores pile up on the kitchen counter instead of handling them like I normally would. I just look at the stack of envelopes and walk right past them.
Have other people, like your wife or coworkers, mentioned that you seem to be moving or speaking more slowly than usual, or on the other hand, that you seem unusually restless or fidgety?

Well, yeah, actually. The guys down at the center have been asking if I'm coming down with something. They say I'm walking a lot slower than usual, and I guess I've been taking forever just to answer simple questions when they ask me stuff on the floor. It just feels like my whole body is trying to move through mud, you know? 

Mud reminds me of this time my buddy Hank got his tractor stuck out in his back field. Hank's got this little hobby farm out past the county line, mostly just grows tomatoes and some sweet corn, but he loves that old John Deere. Anyway, it had been raining for three days straight, just pouring buckets, and he thought he could still get out there to till. Sunk that thing right up to the axles. He had to call his neighbor, old man Peterson, to come pull him out with his heavy-duty Ford. Peterson's a trip, he used to be a rodeo clown back in the seventies. He's got all these crazy stories about dodging angry bulls and hiding in those barrels. Said he broke his collarbone three different times. He actually showed me the X-rays once, keeps them in a manila folder in his glovebox for some reason. I don't know why you'd want to carry around pictures of your broken bones, but I guess everybody's got their quirks. 

But, uh, yeah, moving slow. That's what they tell me at work. Just feel heavy, like I can't get my gears turning right.

He had this old bloodhound named Buster that used to sleep right next to the smoker. Laziest dog you ever saw. One time, a health inspector came by and tried to tell Smitty he couldn't have the dog back there. Smitty just looked at him, didn't say a word, just pointed at the door with his tongs until the guy left. We all laughed about that for weeks. Buster lived to be, gosh, must've been fifteen years old before he finally passed. Smitty actually closed the restaurant for a whole day when it happened. Put a little sign on the door and everything. 

But anyway, they ordered from there last Friday, and I just couldn't do it. The sandwich just sat on my desk all afternoon until I finally threw it in the trash. Same thing at home, really. My wife made her meatloaf on Tuesday, and I just pushed it around my plate. So yeah, I guess my appetite is pretty much gone.

inference.note: Patient endorses depressed mood, anhedonia, appetite/weight loss, and passive suicidal ideation nearly every day for 2 weeks, meeting full criteria for a major depressive episode rather than an adjustment reaction, so F43.2 is now less likely and is dropped. Severity (SI present, functional impact) supports F32.2 over milder classification, with F32.9 retained pending further symptom count (sleep, psychomotor, concentration) and R45.851 retained to code the suicidal ideation itself.

doctor.intent: Assess for feelings of worthlessness or excessive guilt, which help confirm a full major depressive episode versus isolated suicidal ideation
doctor.question: Over these past two weeks, have you been feeling unusually worthless, or blaming yourself for things that aren't really your fault?

target_item.name: Worthlessness_Guilt
target_item.manifestation: I keep going over my daughter leaving and telling myself I must have failed her somehow, like a better father would have done something different.
target_item.reason: The doctor's question specifically asks about feelings of worthlessness and self-blame/guilt, which maps directly to the Worthlessness_Guilt symptom.

patient.answer:
Well, yeah, I guess I have been feeling pretty down on myself. Especially about my daughter. She moved out a while back, and I just keep going over it in my head, telling myself I must have failed her somehow. Like, if I was a better father, I would have done something different, you know? 

She moved out to Seattle, actually. Said she wanted to be closer to the mountains or something. I don't know much about Seattle, except it rains all the time and they've got that big tower with the restaurant on top. My cousin Lou went up there for a convention once—he sells industrial floor buffers, mostly to hospitals and big schools. Lou said the coffee out there is so strong it'll put hair on your chest. He actually brought me back a bag of beans from some little roaster downtown, but I never got around to grinding them. I don't even own a coffee grinder. I just use the Folgers crystals, always have. My dad used to drink Folgers, too. He had this old tin mug he took with him every morning to the auto shop. He dropped a transmission on his foot once, right after he finished his coffee. Didn't even go to the hospital, just taped it up and kept working. Tough old bird, my dad. 

But, uh, yeah, my daughter... I just can't shake this feeling that it's my fault she left. Like I messed up somewhere along the line.

inference.note: Confirmed depressed mood, anhedonia, appetite loss, guilt/worthlessness, and passive SI without plan nearly every day for 2 weeks, meeting most MDD criteria; severity leans major depressive episode (specifying severity pending sleep/psychomotor/concentration data), so F32.9 narrowed toward F32.2/F32.1 depending on final symptom count; R45.851 retained for passive suicidal ideation.

doctor.intent: Assess level of functional impairment and energy/fatigue to help distinguish severity of depressive episode (moderate vs severe) from isolated suicidal ideation
doctor.question: Over these past two weeks, have you noticed feeling unusually tired or low on energy, or having trouble concentrating on tasks at work?

target_item.name: Diminished_Thinking
target_item.manifestation: At the distribution center I stare at the schedule or the routing sheet and my mind just won't lock in, so little staffing calls feel bigger than they ought to.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about trouble concentrating on tasks at work, which directly maps to Diminished Thinking.

patient.answer:
Well, yeah, it's been real tough to focus. Like, at the distribution center, I'll be staring right at the schedule or the routing sheet, and my mind just won't lock in. It's like I'm looking at words but they don't mean anything. So even these little staffing calls, you know, figuring out who's on which shift, they just feel so much bigger and harder than they ought to. 

We had this one guy, Tommy, who used to do the scheduling before me. He was a real character. Always wore these bright yellow suspenders, said they helped him think better. He actually bought them at this little hardware store down in Florida when he was on vacation with his wife. They went to Panama City Beach every single year for their anniversary. Rented the exact same condo on the third floor. Tommy said the elevator in that building was so slow you could read a whole newspaper before you got to the lobby. He used to read the sports section on the way down, always checking the greyhound racing results. Not that he ever bet on them, he just liked the dogs' names. Some of them are real funny, you know? Like "Lightning Bug" or "Salty Biscuit." 

But yeah, I just can't seem to concentrate on the schedules lately. Just feels like my brain is moving through molasses or something.

inference.note: Confirmed additional core depressive symptoms (anhedonia, appetite/weight loss, guilt, concentration difficulty) meeting most DSM/ICD criteria for a major depressive episode; passive suicidal ideation without plan or intent supports R45.851. Severity still needs clarification (psychomotor changes, functional impairment) to differentiate moderate vs severe episode, so both F32.1 and F32.2 remain.

doctor.intent: Assess severity by evaluating functional impairment—specifically whether these symptoms have impaired his ability to perform his job duties or daily responsibilities
doctor.question: Have these feelings and difficulties been severe enough that you've had trouble actually completing your work duties or handling your usual responsibilities at home?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: At work, my mistakes got serious enough that a supervisor found me sitting in my truck before dawn and got occupational health involved. At home, I’ve let bills and responsibilities pile up instead of handling them like I normally would.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the impact of the symptoms on my ability to complete work duties and handle responsibilities at home, which corresponds to functional impairment.

patient.answer:
Yeah, it's... it's gotten pretty bad, to be honest. At work, my mistakes started getting serious enough that my supervisor actually found me just sitting out in my truck before dawn one morning. He ended up getting occupational health involved, which was a whole embarrassing ordeal. I was just sitting in the cab, not even with the radio on, you know? 

It's a Chevy Silverado. Good truck. I bought it off this fella named Al over at the dealership on Route 9. Al was a real trip, he always wore these ridiculous neckties. The day I bought the truck, he had on this tie with little singing bass fish all over it. Reminded me of my brother-in-law, Gary. Gary is obsessed with fishing. He goes up to the lake every August, rents this little cabin that doesn't even have indoor plumbing. Just an outhouse out back. I told him he's crazy for paying good money to use a hole in the ground, but he says it builds character. He actually caught this massive catfish last year and had it stuffed and mounted right above his TV in the living room. His wife hates it, says its glass eyes follow her around when she's vacuuming. She tried to throw it out once when he was at work, but it wouldn't fit in the trash can. 

But, uh... anyway, what was I saying? Oh, right, my responsibilities. Yeah, it's the same thing at home, really. I’ve just let all the bills and my regular chores pile up on the kitchen counter instead of handling them like I normally would. I just look at the stack of envelopes and walk right past them.

inference.note: The patient now reports clear functional impairment at both work (errors requiring occupational health involvement) and home (neglected bills/chores), consistent with a severe (not moderate) depressive episode. This rules out F32.1, leaving F32.2 as the primary diagnosis, with R45.851 retained to code the passive suicidal ideation without plan or intent.

doctor.intent: Assess for psychomotor changes (agitation or retardation) noticeable to others, to complete the criteria set for a major depressive episode and support/refute F32.2 over an isolated symptom code (R45.851)
doctor.question: Have other people, like your wife or coworkers, mentioned that you seem to be moving or speaking more slowly than usual, or on the other hand, that you seem unusually restless or fidgety?

target_item.name: Psychomotor_Changes
target_item.manifestation: People at work keep asking if I'm sick because I'm walking slower, taking forever to answer simple questions, and feeling like my body is moving through mud.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about observable changes in movement or speech (moving/speaking slowly or being restless/fidgety), which aligns with psychomotor changes.

patient.answer:
Well, yeah, actually. The guys down at the center have been asking if I'm coming down with something. They say I'm walking a lot slower than usual, and I guess I've been taking forever just to answer simple questions when they ask me stuff on the floor. It just feels like my whole body is trying to move through mud, you know? 

Mud reminds me of this time my buddy Hank got his tractor stuck out in his back field. Hank's got this little hobby farm out past the county line, mostly just grows tomatoes and some sweet corn, but he loves that old John Deere. Anyway, it had been raining for three days straight, just pouring buckets, and he thought he could still get out there to till. Sunk that thing right up to the axles. He had to call his neighbor, old man Peterson, to come pull him out with his heavy-duty Ford. Peterson's a trip, he used to be a rodeo clown back in the seventies. He's got all these crazy stories about dodging angry bulls and hiding in those barrels. Said he broke his collarbone three different times. He actually showed me the X-rays once, keeps them in a manila folder in his glovebox for some reason. I don't know why you'd want to carry around pictures of your broken bones, but I guess everybody's got their quirks. 

But, uh, yeah, moving slow. That's what they tell me at work. Just feel heavy, like I can't get my gears turning right.

inference.note: Patient endorses depressed mood, anhedonia, appetite loss, worthlessness/guilt, concentration difficulty, psychomotor retardation observed by others, and passive suicidal ideation without plan, all nearly daily for 2 weeks, meeting criteria for a single major depressive episode, severe, without psychotic features. Passive SI (R45.851) is now subsumed as a symptom criterion of the major depressive episode rather than a standalone diagnosis, and no additional features suggest psychosis, mania, or another disorder.

opening_question.intent: Identify the primary reason for the visit
opening_question.question: Hi, welcome in—I'm Dr. [Name]. To start, can you tell me what brings you in today?
